_meta.domain: Include a person only if a historically significant part of that person's scientific contribution is directly to geodesy and measurement of the Earth's figure, gravity field or deformation; seismology, earthquake physics or inference of the Earth's internal structure; geomagnetism, paleomagnetism or the geodynamo; meteorology, atmospheric dynamics, atmospheric composition, weather prediction or physical climate science; physical or chemical oceanography and ocean circulation; hydrology, hydrogeology, groundwater, catchment processes or river hydrology; glaciology, ice-sheet physics, the cryosphere or ice-core climate reconstruction; volcanology, volcanic hazards, geothermal heat flow or the physical and geochemical study of active volcanic systems; or solar-terrestrial and near-space science including the ionosphere, aurora, magnetosphere, radiation belts, solar wind, heliosphere and Sun-Earth coupling. Include measurement, observing systems, remote sensing and instrumentation only when the person's major scientific significance lies in using or creating them to establish knowledge of the Earth, ocean, atmosphere, cryosphere or near-Earth space. Reject anyone whose principal significance lies in any other field. Reject descriptive geologists, stratigraphers, mineralogists and palaeontologists without a substantive geophysical, hydrological, atmospheric, oceanographic, cryospheric or volcanic-process contribution; astronomers, astrophysicists and cosmologists concerned primarily with stars, galaxies, compact objects, the wider universe or planetary bodies rather than the Sun-Earth system and near-Earth space; planetary scientists whose principal subject is another planet, moon or small body rather than Earth or Sun-Earth coupling; physicists and chemists whose work lacks a central Earth, ocean, atmosphere, cryosphere or near-space application; mathematicians and statisticians whose significance is methodological rather than an Earth-system discovery; human, cultural and economic geographers; explorers, surveyors and cartographers whose significance lies principally in travel, territorial mapping, navigation or imperial administration rather than quantitative Earth measurement; civil, mining, petroleum and other engineers whose principal contribution is infrastructure, extraction or industrial technology rather than Earth-system science; environmental policymakers, conservationists and climate advocates without a substantive original scientific contribution; biologists, ecologists and other life scientists whose principal work concerns organisms or ecosystems rather than physical or chemical Earth-system processes; and inventors, administrators or industrialists whose importance is primarily institutional, commercial or technological rather than scientific.
_meta.name: earth and space sciences
